The “Magic Point Shop” of QMC point generators and generating vectors

This page lists both experimental and production code for applying a quasi-Monte Carlo method. Two types of QMC methods are supported:

  • Rank 1 Lattice rules and lattice sequences (in base 2) including higher order versions.
  • Digital nets and digital sequences (in base 2) including higher order versions (aka generalized nets).

This page is in tandem with the QMC4PDE construction codes which allow to construct generating vectors and generating matrices for integrands which have a natural structure coming from PDEs with random diffusion coefficients. Please consult that website for further information on how we characterize such integrands.

Several generating vectors can be found on this web page. All lattice rules and sequences were generated by my fast component-by-component constructions. The Matlab version of those scripts can be found on their own page: fast component-by-component Matlab/Octave scripts.

A more modern implementation of the fast component-by-component algorithms, with different features, in Python2/3 can be obtained from the QMC4PDE project page. The source of those construction scripts are also available from the QMC4PDE git repository.

Similarly, the point generators from this page are also available as a qmc-generators git repository. There is some additional code which can be found on the git repository pages. Some older code is also linked from the current page.

You can download the new QMC4PDE generators as a package. The current version of the Magic Point Shop qmc-generators package is 14 Dec 2017.

Download qmc-generators-20171214.tgz.
Optional download Sobol matrices (including higher order) (large file 21 MB).
Optional download Niederreiter-Xing matrices (including higher order).

If you use this code in your research then please cite on of the related papers. If you don't know which one to cite then you can cite the origin of the current point generators which come form the QMC4PDE project:

F.Y. Kuo & D. Nuyens. Application of quasi-Monte Carlo methods to elliptic PDEs with random diffusion coefficients - a survey of analysis and implementation, Foundations of Computational Mathematics, 16(6):1631-1696, 2016. (springer link, arxiv link)

The vectors for the Niederreiter-Xing sequence have been obtained from Pirsic's website. The code necessary to convert and assemble the generating matrices from Pirsic's website into a suitable generating vector (consisting of generating matrices) is provided. Also generating vectors for the Sobol' sequence are provided. These have been obtained from Kuo's website.

The typical convergence obtained using QMC points is near O(N−1). In classical s dimensional function spaces there is a (log N)s factor, while in appropriately weighted function spaces this exponential dependency on the number of dimensions can be removed. This website is however just about software to generate QMC points, the warnings are in the fine print of your receipt… (You might consult this article by F. Y. Kuo and Ian H. Sloan in AMS Notices to learn more about weighted function spaces and tractability.)

If the function is sufficiently smooth then it is also possible to achieve higher order of convergence O(N−α. The code on this page is also capable of generating higher order lattice rules (and sequences) and higher order digital nets (and sequences). One only has to initialize the point generator with a higher order generating vector. The generator will then deliver the correct points. For lattice rules this is naturally done with the same code, while the digital nets and sequence code is written in such a way that higher order generating vectors have the correct effect.

Currently all code on this page is concerned with sequences in base 2 as this is the most efficient case to implement and as such also the most interesting case for practitioners.

NB: If you notice any errors or inaccuracies in the code or on this page, please do not hesitate to email me. I am also happy to answer any usage related questions you might have.

Lattice sequences in base 2

Given a generating vector z of integers, the kth point of the sequence is given by

xk := φ(k) z mod 1, for k=0,1,2,…,

where φ is typically the radical inverse or the gray coded radical inverse function in the base of the lattice sequence.

The radical inverse of an integer k with m digit base b expansion

k = (km-1 km-2 ⋯ k0)b
is obtained by mirroring the digits at the fractional point, i.e.,
φ(k) = (0.k0 k1 ⋯ km-1)b .
Obviously the result is a rational in bm and an alternative view is thus to look at this mapping as a permutation of the integers in {0,…,bm−1}. In other words we are reversing the digits. Luckily, in base 2 reversing digits can be done efficiently. At the end of this section there is a Matlab/Octave and a C++ version to reverse bits. To obtain the radical inverse in base 2 of an unsigned 32 bit integer then just requires scaling the result of the bit reversion by 2−32.

Working in gray code ordering has speed advantages for digital nets (and sequences) but less so for lattice sequences.

NOTE: although below are links to source code it is better to consult the qmc-generators git repository which contains the same source code and additional examples and explanations.

The following Matlab/Octave scripts are available (related to the QMC4PDE project):

  1. matlab/latticeseq_b2.m: lattice sequence point generator in radical inverse order
  2. matlab/bitreverse32.m: bit reversion of 32 bit unsigned integers

The following C++ generators are available (related to the QMC4PDE project):

  1. cpp/latticeseq_b2.hpp: you can use this class in your own code.
  2. cpp/latticeseq_b2.cpp: this is an example command line point generator using the previous header file.
  3. Two example files to integrate a 100-dimensional function are also provided: cpp/example_01.cpp and cpp/example_02.cpp. These examples and how to use the point generators is well documented by navigating to the cpp directory of the qmc-generators git repository.

The following Python2/3 code is available (related to the QMC4PDE project):

  1. python/latticeseq_b2.py: this file contains a point generator class for use in your own code and also has a main method such that it can also be ran as a command line point generator.

Here is a small list of generating vectors for lattice sequences in base 2 in the directory LATSEQ. They were all generated by my fast component-by-component algorithms.

  1. exod2_base2_m20_CKN: The 250-dimensional base-2 generating vector for order-2 weights up to 220 = 1048576 points from the Cools, Kuo and Nuyens SIAM SISC paper (2006).
  2. exod2_base2_m20: A 600-dimensional base-2 generating vector for order-2 weights up to 220 = 1048576 points.
  3. exod2_base2_m13: A 600-dimensional base-2 generating vector for order-2 weights up to 213 = 8192 points.
  4. exod8_base2_m13: A 600-dimensional base-2 generating vector for order-8 weights (all 1) up to 213 = 8192 points.
  5. exew_base2_m20_a3_HKKN.txt: A 10-dimensional base-2 generating vector for an equal weight (all one) Korobov space with optimal rate N-3 up to 220 = 1048576 points from Hickernell, Kritzer, Kuo and Nuyens (2011) - Weighted compound integration rules with higher order convergence for all N.

For randomization one uses Cranley-Patterson shifting:

  1. matlab/mod1shift.m

Digital sequences in base 2

Digital sequences are not generated by an integer generating vector as is the case for lattice sequences, but they are generated by a set of generating matrices. Here we think of them as a vector of matrices. These are matrices with elements from a finite field. For a digital sequence in base 2 this finite field is simply Z2.

NOTE: although below are links to source code it is better to consult the qmc-generators git repository which contains the same source code and additional examples and explanations.

The following Matlab/Octave scripts are available (related to the QMC4PDE project):

  1. matlab/digitalseq_b2g.m: digital sequence point generator in radical inverse gray code order
  2. matlab/bitreverse64.m: bit reversion of 64 bit unsigned integers

The following C++ generators are available (related to the QMC4PDE project):

  1. cpp/digitalseq_b2g.hpp: you can use this class in your own code.
  2. cpp/digitalseq_b2g.cpp: this is an example command line point generator using the previous header file.

The following Python2/3 code is available (related to the QMC4PDE project):

  1. python/digitalseq_b2g.py: this file contains a point generator class for use in your own code and also has a main method such that it can also be ran as a command line point generator.

The following older C++ programs to convert and assemble generating matrices from Pirsic's website are also still available:

  1. row2full.cc: given a matrix in the format from Pirsic this writes the full matrix as an array of zeros and ones; similar to the libseq format (which can be found in the archive to generate the points).
  2. compact_matrices.cc: given a matrix in the format of the libseq code this program will print out an integer for every column in a generating matrix in the format needed for the Matlab point generator.
  3. homerge.cc: this program implements Josef Dick's explicit higher order construction based on generating matrices in the libseq format as outputted by the row2full program.

There is a collection of generating matrices for digital sequences (in base 2) in the directory DIGSEQ. Matrices for Niederreiter-Xing digital sequences and higher order sequences constructed on the basis of these matrices can be found in the directory DIGSEQ/nxmats. Similarly we provide generating matrices for the Sobol' sequence corresponding to the Joe and Kuo paper in ACM Transactions om Mathematical Software can be found in the DIGSEQ/sobolmats directory. You can also download sobolmats.tgz. All of these come in plain vanilla or higher order versions.

For randomization one can use digital shifting:

  1. matlab/digitalshift.m
